A vent is an opening — a hole, gap, or passage — through which something can pass through or escape. That "something" is usually air, gas, smoke, liquid, or even emotion. The opening exists on purpose: it is there to allow or control that movement.
Meaning 1: An opening that lets air or gas pass through

This is the most common meaning you will encounter in everyday life.

A vent is any intentional hole or opening built into a structure to allow air, gas, smoke, or similar substances to flow in or out. The key word is intentional — a vent is not an accidental crack; it is designed with a function in mind.

Examples:

  • The grille-covered opening in your wall or ceiling connected to your home's heating or air conditioning system is an air vent. Warm or cool air flows through it into your room.
  • A kitchen stove has a vent (or is connected to one above it) that carries cooking fumes and smoke outside.
  • Cars have vents on the dashboard that direct airflow into the cabin — you can usually tilt or close these.
  • An underground tunnel or mine has vents to bring in fresh air and push out stale, dangerous air.

The underlying purpose is always the same: to relieve pressure, improve circulation, or safely remove something that would otherwise build up and cause harm.
Meaning 2: A slit in a garment

In clothing, a vent is a vertical cut or slit made at the back (or sides) of a jacket, blazer, coat, or skirt — usually at the lower hem.

You may have noticed that the back of a formal suit jacket often has one or two narrow slits at the bottom. Those are vents. They are there for the same reason as an air vent: to open things up. Without them, the fabric would pull and restrict your movement every time you walked or sat down. The vent lets the garment move with your body.

  • A single vent = one slit in the center back of a jacket.
  • Double vents (or side vents) = two slits, one on each side.
  • No vent = a completely closed back; a cleaner look but slightly less comfortable.

In geology, a vent is the opening through which a volcano releases its contents — lava, ash, gases, and steam — to the surface. It is essentially the "mouth" or "outlet" of the volcano. A volcano can have one main vent at its peak and several smaller secondary vents on its sides.

A related term you may come across is a hydrothermal vent. This is an opening on the deep ocean floor through which geothermally heated water (and dissolved minerals) shoots out. These vents exist because of volcanic activity beneath the seafloor. What makes them remarkable is that despite the total darkness and extreme pressure, entire ecosystems of unusual creatures — tube worms, blind shrimp, giant clams — thrive around them. They do not depend on sunlight at all.
Meaning 4: The vent of a bird, reptile, fish, or amphibian

In biology, the vent refers to the single external opening found in birds, reptiles, amphibians, and many fish, located at the base of the tail. It is the one opening through which the digestive, urinary, and reproductive systems all empty.

For example:

  • A bird's vent is used for eliminating waste and for laying eggs.
  • Reptiles like lizards and snakes have a similar vent, also called the cloaca.

Mammals (including humans) have these functions separated into distinct openings; in birds and reptiles, nature has combined them into one: the vent.
Meaning 5: A vent as an outlet for emotion

"Vent" is also used as a noun to describe an outlet for strong feelings — typically frustration, anger, or pent-up stress.

In this sense, a vent functions just like a physical vent: it releases pressure that has built up inside. When something has been bottled up for too long, a vent provides an escape route.

This meaning most often appears in the phrase "give vent to" something, which means to express or release a feeling you have been holding back.

Examples:

  • "She finally gave vent to years of frustration in that one conversation."
  • "Writing in his journal was a vent for all his unexpressed anger."
  • "He had no vent for his grief — no one to talk to, no way to let it out."

You will also encounter this sense in everyday speech with the verb form ("I just need to vent"), but as a noun, the phrasing "give vent to" is what to watch for in writing.
Meaning 6: The vent of a cannon (historical)

In older weapons such as cannons or early firearms, the vent (sometimes also called the touch-hole) was a tiny hole at the rear end of the barrel. Gunpowder was ignited by inserting a flame or spark through this vent hole, which would then fire the weapon. Though this meaning is largely historical and you are unlikely to encounter it outside of books set in earlier centuries, it follows the same logic: a small opening through which something (here, fire) passes.
The single idea that ties all meanings together

No matter the context, a vent is always some kind of opening or outlet — something that allows a substance or force to pass through, escape, or be released. Whether it is air flowing through a wall, lava escaping a volcano, a slit in a jacket giving room to move, waste leaving a bird's body, or grief finally finding expression — in every case, something that was enclosed or under pressure finds a way out.

That is the word in full.
